easy.prompt: An algorithm performs 4n + 7 elementary steps on inputs of size n. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It performs at most c·n steps for large n (some constant c).

choices.label: B
choices.body: It performs exactly 4n + 7 steps on every input.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It performs at least c·n steps for large n.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It performs 4n + 7 steps on average over random inputs.

easy.hint: Next step: compare the step count against c·n for large n — can you find a c that always stays above 4n+7?
easy.explanation: O(n) means the step count is bounded above by a constant times n for large n; it hides the 4 and the +7.
easy.deepDive: Big-O is an upper bound up to constants: drop the lower-order +7 and the leading 4 to get O(n). The constant c absorbs the 4 and the +7 for all n beyond some n0. So O(n) claims growth is at most linear, nothing about exact counts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Big-O hides constants and lower-order terms; it never reports an exact step count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes a lower bound (Big-Omega), not an upper bound (Big-O).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Big-O alone is a worst-case asymptotic bound, not an average over random inputs.

easy.prompt: What does the formal statement f(n) = O(g(n)) mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: There exist c > 0 and n0 with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.

choices.label: B
choices.body: f(n) ≤ g(n) for every n, with no constant allowed.

choices.label: C
choices.body: f(n) / g(n) → 0 as n → ∞.

choices.label: D
choices.body: f(n) = c·g(n) for some fixed c and all n.

easy.hint: Next step: write down the inequality with an unknown c and n0, then try to satisfy it for large n.
easy.explanation: That is the textbook definition of Big-O: an upper bound up to a constant factor beyond some threshold n0.
easy.deepDive: The formal definition lets c absorb leading constants (e.g., 5n ≤ 6·n for n ≥ 1) and n0 ignore small inputs where lower-order terms dominate. Option B fails because 5n ≤ n is false even though 5n = O(n). Option C defines little-o, a strictly stronger claim. So always test the c/n0 form on large n.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Big-O explicitly allows a constant factor c; without it almost nothing like 5n = O(n) would hold.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is little-o (strictly smaller), not Big-O (at most as big).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Big-O is an inequality for large n, not an exact equality for all n.

easy.prompt: What does f(n) = Ω(g(n)) mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A lower bound: g grows at least as fast as f, up to constants.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An upper bound: g grows at most as fast as f, up to constants.

choices.label: C
choices.body: An exact count of steps the algorithm performs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An average-case bound over random inputs.

easy.hint: Next step: flip the Big-O inequality — ask whether f stays ABOVE some constant multiple of g.
easy.explanation: Big-Omega is a lower bound up to constant factors: f grows at least as fast as g.
easy.deepDive: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all large n — g is a floor on f's growth. Example: 3n² + n ≥ 3n², so it is Ω(n²). This is the mirror image of Big-O, which puts a ceiling instead. Confusing the two flips every comparison.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is Big-O (upper bound); Omega is the reverse inequality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Asymptotic notation hides constants and never gives exact counts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Omega alone says nothing about averaging; it bounds growth for large n.

easy.prompt: What does f(n) = Θ(g(n)) mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: f is both O(g) and Ω(g): the two bound f tightly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: f is O(g) but definitely not Ω(g).

choices.label: C
choices.body: f equals g on every input size n.

choices.label: D
choices.body: f is the running time and g is the input size.

easy.hint: Next step: split the claim in two — check the O direction, then check the Omega direction.
easy.explanation: Theta is the tight bound: O and Omega simultaneously, pinning growth up to constants.
easy.deepDive: Theta means two one-sided bounds hold at once: c₁g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂g(n) for large n. Example: 3n² + 10n sits between 3n² and 23n² for n ≥ 1, hence Θ(n²). Either half alone (O or Ω) is weaker; Theta is their conjunction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is little-o territory; Theta requires the Omega half too.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Theta allows constant-factor slack, so exact equality is far stronger than needed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Theta relates two growth functions, not a time to an input size per se.

easy.prompt: Solve T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(1) with T(0) = Θ(1).

choices.label: A
choices.body: Θ(n): n unit-cost calls in a chain.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Θ(log n): the input halves each call.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Θ(n²): each call repeats all prior work.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Θ(1): recursion is always constant time.

easy.hint: Next step: unroll the recurrence twice and count how many levels appear before hitting T(0).
easy.explanation: One smaller subproblem plus constant work per level over n levels sums to Θ(n).
easy.deepDive: Unroll T(n) = T(n−1) + c: each level strips one element at cost c, forming a chain of n levels. Total = c·n = Θ(n). There is no halving here (that would give log n) and no growing per-level cost (that would give n²).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nothing halves; the argument drops by 1, giving n levels, not log n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Per-level cost is constant, not growing, so the sum is linear, not quadratic.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Recursion depth is n here, so total work grows with n.

easy.prompt: In the recursion tree for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), what is the work per level?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Θ(n) work per level across Θ(log n) levels.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Θ(1) work per level across Θ(n) levels.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Θ(n²) work on a single level.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Θ(log n) work per level across Θ(n) levels.

easy.hint: Next step: compute level i's total as (number of nodes) × (cost per node).
easy.explanation: Each of the log n levels splits n work evenly, so per-level work is Θ(n).
easy.deepDive: Level i has 2^i nodes each costing n/2^i, so every level sums to exactly n. Depth is log₂n since n halves log₂n times before reaching 1. Multiplying Θ(n) per level by Θ(log n) levels gives Θ(n log n), the mergesort bound.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The input halves (log n levels), and each level carries the full n work.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Work is spread evenly over log n levels; no single level does n² work.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Level count is logarithmic and per-level work is linear — this swaps the two.

easy.prompt: Which recurrence is in Master-theorem form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)?
easy.hint: Next step: check each option for the single pattern aT(n/b) — does every recursive call use the same divisor b?
easy.explanation: Master form requires a copies of size n/b for fixed a ≥ 1, b > 1 — only the mergesort recurrence qualifies.
easy.deepDive: Master needs T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1, b > 1: one subproblem size n/b repeated a times. Only option A has that shape (a = 2, b = 2). Options B and D subtract instead of dividing, and C has two different divisors, so none fit the required single-fraction form.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Subtracting 1 is not dividing by b; Master needs n/b with b > 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Two different fractions (n/3 and 2n/3) break the single-b requirement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Fibonacci-style subtraction never fits the divide-by-b form.

easy.prompt: Apply the Master theorem to T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n).

choices.label: A
choices.body: Θ(n log n)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Θ(n)

choices.label: C
choices.body: Θ(n²)

choices.label: D
choices.body: Θ(log n)

easy.hint: Next step: compute n^{log_b a} and compare it with f(n) — equal, bigger, or smaller?
easy.explanation: n^{log₂2} = n matches f(n) = Θ(n) (case 2), so the answer is Θ(n log n).
easy.deepDive: Here a = 2, b = 2 so n^{log_b a} = n^1 = n, and f(n) = Θ(n) matches it exactly — Master case 2. Case 2 adds a log factor: T(n) = Θ(n log n). This is the mergesort recurrence: linear combine work on log n even levels.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is case 1 (f smaller); here f equals n^{log_b a}, not smaller.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Quadratic would need n^{log_b a} = n² or dominating f, neither holds.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Logarithmic would need a single unit-cost branch, but a = 2 here.

easy.prompt: Which dynamic-array operation is O(1) amortized?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Appending to the end (push back).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Inserting at the front.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deleting from the middle.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Searching for an arbitrary value.

easy.hint: Next step: total the cost of n appends including resizes, then divide by n.
easy.explanation: Doubling makes expensive resizes exponentially rare, so end-appends average to O(1) each.
easy.deepDive: Appends are usually O(1); only the append that exhausts capacity pays Θ(n) to copy into a doubled array. Since capacity doubles each resize, resize costs n + 2n + 4n + … form a geometric series bounded by 2n over n appends. Hence O(1) amortized per append despite occasional expensive ones.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Front insertion shifts all n elements every time: Θ(n), not amortized-constant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mid-deletion also shifts Θ(n) elements on every call.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Unordered search scans Θ(n) elements regardless of amortization.

easy.prompt: A recursive linear search checks the first element, then recurses on the rest. What recurrence describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(1): one smaller instance plus constant work.

choices.label: B
choices.body: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n): two halves plus linear work.

choices.label: C
choices.body: T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n): one smaller instance plus linear work.

choices.label: D
choices.body: T(n) = Θ(1): no recursion at all.

easy.hint: Next step: count the recursive calls per invocation and the size each one handles.
easy.explanation: One recursive call on n−1 elements plus one comparison gives T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(1).
easy.deepDive: A linear scan checks s[0], then recurses on the remaining n−1 characters: one subproblem of size n−1. The per-call work (one comparison) is Θ(1). So the structure is exactly T(n) = T(n−1) + Θ(1), which solves to Θ(n). No splitting or linear scan per call occurs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nothing splits in half here; there is one call on n−1, not two on n/2.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Per-call work is one comparison, not a scan of all n elements.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The function calls itself on smaller input, so recursion is present.

easy.prompt: Counting nodes in a full binary tree by recursing on both subtrees gives which recurrence?

choices.label: A
choices.body: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(1): split in half, recurse both sides, O(1) combine.

choices.label: B
choices.body: T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1): search one half only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(1): strip one element.

choices.label: D
choices.body: T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + Θ(1): two calls each stripping one element.

easy.hint: Next step: ask how many recursive calls fire per node and what size each receives.
easy.explanation: Both halves are visited after O(1) work at the node: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(1).
easy.deepDive: Counting nodes in a full binary tree visits the root (O(1)), then recurses on both halves of size n/2. That is two subproblems of size n/2 with constant combine work. Note this differs from binary search, which discards one half and makes one call. Here both halves are explored.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One call on half the input is binary search; counting visits both halves.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Stripping one element is linear search, not tree halving.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Each subtree has size n/2, not n−1; nothing strips a single element.

easy.prompt: What does the recursion tree of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) look like?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Depth Θ(log n), Θ(n) nodes per level at the top.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Depth Θ(n), one node per level.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Depth Θ(log n), one node per level.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Depth Θ(n log n) with Θ(n) nodes per level.

easy.hint: Next step: draw levels 0, 1, 2 — count nodes and write each node's input size.
easy.explanation: Halving depth (log n) with doubling breadth gives a full tree: Θ(n) nodes-content per level.
easy.deepDive: Each level doubles the node count while halving sizes: level i has 2^i nodes of size n/2^i. Depth is log₂n since halving reaches 1 after log n steps. Near the root each level holds Θ(n) total elements across its nodes. This even, full tree is the mergesort shape yielding Θ(n log n).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One node per level is a chain (T(n−1)); here nodes double each level.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Single-node levels describe binary search (one call); this makes two calls.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Depth is logarithmic, not n log n; halving reaches 1 in log n steps.

easy.prompt: What does the recursion tree of T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n) sum to?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A chain of n levels: total Θ(n²).

choices.label: B
choices.body: A balanced tree of log n levels: total Θ(n log n).

choices.label: C
choices.body: A star: root plus n leaves, total Θ(n).

choices.label: D
choices.body: A single node: total Θ(1).

easy.hint: Next step: unroll three levels and stack the costs vertically — what series appears?
easy.explanation: n levels with costs n, n−1, …, 1 form an arithmetic series summing to Θ(n²).
easy.deepDive: Unrolling T(n) = T(n−1) + n peels one element per level, so depth is n and level i costs n−i. Summing n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2 gives Θ(n²). No branching means no tree width — just a chain with growing per-level cost.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Balanced halving needs n/2 subproblems; here size drops by 1, giving n levels.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Every level has exactly one node (one call), not n parallel leaves.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The chain has n levels of growing cost, far more than one node.

easy.prompt: What is the standard variable/value ordering for backtracking search (e.g., N-queens, Sudoku)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Order variables by fewest remaining values; try values least constraining first.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always pick variables alphabetically and values numerically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Pick the variable with the most remaining values first.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assign all variables, then check constraints once at the end.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which unassigned variable would detect a contradiction soonest.
easy.explanation: Constrained variables first fail fast; permissive values first succeed fast — both shrink the searched tree.
easy.deepDive: Fail-first ordering (minimum remaining values) exposes dead ends early, pruning whole subtrees before they are built. Least-constraining values keep future options open, finding solutions faster. Alphabetical order ignores constraint tightness, and checking only at the end (generate-and-test) explores the full exponential space. Ordering never changes correctness, only search size.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fixed orders ignore tightness; they find dead ends late instead of early.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Most-options-first explores the bushiest subtrees before constrained ones — backwards.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: End-only checking is generate-and-test; it forfeits all early pruning.

easy.prompt: How does value ordering affect a backtracking search?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It can only shrink the explored tree, never change the answer set.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It changes which solutions exist.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It guarantees polynomial running time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It requires storing every visited state.

easy.hint: Next step: consider the full search tree — does reordering branches delete any leaf?
easy.explanation: Ordering rearranges traversal without removing solutions; it only affects how soon search succeeds or fails.
easy.deepDive: Trying values in a different order visits the same solution set in a different sequence — completeness is preserved. Good orders reach solutions (or contradictions) after fewer nodes. But worst case stays exponential: ordering prunes, it does not collapse complexity classes. And no extra memory is implied.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The solution set is fixed by constraints; ordering only reorders exploration.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Worst case remains exponential; ordering is a heuristic, not a complexity cure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Ordering needs no storage; memoization (distinct technique) stores states.

easy.prompt: In branch-and-bound maximization, a node's optimistic upper bound is ≤ the best solution so far. What should you do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Abandon the node: no completion can beat the best known.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Explore it fully: bounds are only advisory.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Restart search from the root.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Double the bound and continue.

easy.hint: Next step: compare the node's ceiling against your best solution — can anything underneath win?
easy.explanation: An optimistic bound at or below the incumbent proves the subtree is useless — prune it soundly.
easy.deepDive: Branch-and-bound keeps the best feasible value B* and an optimistic bound U(node) ≥ any completion's value. If U(node) ≤ B*, the subtree provably contains nothing better, so pruning is sound. Exploring it anyway wastes exponential work; restarting or loosening the bound discards the information already earned.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Full exploration of a provably useless subtree wastes the savings bounding exists for.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Restarting throws away the incumbent and all bounds computed so far.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Inflating the bound destroys its validity; bounds must stay optimistic-but-sound.

easy.prompt: What makes a branch-and-bound bound valid for pruning?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A valid bound must be optimistic (never exclude a better solution) to prune soundly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Any bound, even a pessimistic guess, prunes soundly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bounds must equal the exact optimum to be usable.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bounds only apply at leaf nodes.

easy.hint: Next step: ask what happens to the true optimum if your bound is too low and you prune on it.
easy.explanation: Pruning is sound only if the bound never underestimates the subtree's potential (maximization).
easy.deepDive: Soundness requires U(node) ≥ true best completion (for maximization): pruning when U ≤ B* then provably discards nothing better. A pessimistic 'bound' below the true value would prune the optimum — the classic unsound-pruning bug. Exact optima as bounds would be ideal but are as hard as the problem; relaxations (e.g., fractional knapsack) give cheap optimism.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Pessimistic bounds prune the optimum itself — the worst possible bug.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Exact bounds are unnecessary; cheap optimistic relaxations are the standard tool.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bounds are most useful at internal nodes, cutting whole subtrees before descent.

easy.prompt: What does an explicit base case guarantee for a recursive function?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Terminates: input shrinks toward a stated base case on every path.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Correct: the code compiles without errors.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Fast: it runs in polynomial time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Safe: it never uses extra memory.

easy.hint: Next step: trace the argument values along one call chain — do they hit the base case?
easy.explanation: Base cases plus ever-shrinking arguments guarantee the recursion bottoms out.
easy.deepDive: A base case anchors the recursion and a shrinking argument guarantees reaching it — together they prove termination. Compilation, speed, and memory are separate concerns a base case cannot certify. When reviewing recursion, first check: is there a base case, and does every call move toward it?

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Compiling is syntax; base cases are about runtime termination semantics.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Termination says nothing about speed — naive Fibonacci terminates yet is exponential.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Call-stack memory grows with depth regardless of base cases existing.

easy.prompt: Which two properties make a problem suitable for dynamic programming?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sorted input + numeric output.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A greedy choice at every step.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random sampling of states.

easy.hint: Next step: check two things — do recursive calls repeat states, and does the optimum use smaller optima?
easy.explanation: DP applies when subproblems repeat (memoization helps) and optima compose from smaller optima.
easy.deepDive: Overlapping subproblems mean naive recursion recomputes the same states (fib(3) inside fib(5) many times), so caching pays. Optimal substructure means optima build from optima of smaller states (fib(5) from fib(4), fib(3)). Sorted input, greediness, and randomness are unrelated; many DP problems are unordered and exact.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DP needs structural properties, not sortedness or numeric answers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Always-greedy is the greedy precondition, strictly stronger than DP needs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DP is exact and exhaustive over states, not sampling-based.

easy.prompt: What does 'defining the subproblems' mean in DP?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The set of distinct states plus their dependency (transition) structure.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The programming language used to implement the solver.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The number of test cases in the judge.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The recursion depth limit of the machine.

easy.hint: Next step: write the parameters that uniquely identify one smaller instance of your problem.
easy.explanation: A subproblem definition names all states and how each depends on smaller ones.
easy.deepDive: Defining states means naming every distinct subproblem (e.g., fib(k) for k ≤ n; knapsack(i, w) for items and capacities). Transitions say how each state derives from smaller ones. This pair fixes table size and per-cell work, hence total complexity. Language, test counts, and stack limits are implementation details, not the subproblem definition.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Language choice never changes the state space or transitions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Test counts are external; states are intrinsic to the problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Stack limits constrain implementation, not the mathematical subproblems.

easy.prompt: What distinguishes memoized (top-down) DP from tabular (bottom-up) DP?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Top-down computes lazily via recursion + cache; bottom-up fills the table iteratively.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Top-down uses no extra memory; bottom-up uses a table.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Top-down is always asymptotically faster.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Bottom-up only works for greedy problems.

easy.hint: Next step: ask which states each style touches — only reachable ones, or the whole table?
easy.explanation: Same table, two fill orders: demand-driven recursion versus systematic iteration.
easy.deepDive: Memoized top-down starts from the goal state and recurses only into reachable substates, caching each. Bottom-up iterates over the full table in dependency order, touching every cell including unreachable ones. Both store results (same memory order) and share asymptotics; they differ in laziness vs. iteration, and in stack-vs-loop overhead.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both store subproblem results; memoization's cache is also extra memory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Asymptotics match; only constants and reachable-state counts differ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bottom-up solves the same DP problems, not greedy ones.

easy.prompt: When does memoized recursion beat bottom-up tabulation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Top-down may touch fewer states; bottom-up touches the whole table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Top-down always uses less memory.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Bottom-up can never be space-optimized.

choices.label: D
choices.body: They compute different answers.

easy.hint: Next step: shade which table cells the goal state can actually reach through transitions.
easy.explanation: Laziness skips unreachable states; full tabulation does not — the key practical difference.
easy.deepDive: Lazy recursion explores only states reachable from the goal (e.g., sparse knapsack capacities actually visited). Bottom-up loops visit every cell by construction. Memory can favor either side: bottom-up often compresses to rows (edit distance to one row), while top-down keeps a sparse cache plus call stack. Both are exact — same recurrence, same answer.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Top-down adds call-stack overhead and a cache; memory winner depends on the problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Row-compression (keeping one previous row) is a classic bottom-up saving.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both evaluate the same recurrence, so answers agree by construction.

easy.prompt: What makes a bottom-up evaluation order valid?

choices.label: A
choices.body: An order where every transition reads already-computed (smaller) states.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Alphabetical order of variable names.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decreasing order of answer values.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Random order with retries.

easy.hint: Next step: draw one transition's arrows and check they point backward to finished cells.
easy.explanation: Valid orders respect dependencies: smaller states before the larger states built on them.
easy.deepDive: Bottom-up is correct iff dependencies resolve first: for LIS increasing i works since L(i) reads j < i; for knapsack increasing i then w works since (i,w) reads row i−1. Alphabetical, value-sorted, and random orders ignore the dependency DAG and read uninitialized cells. The order is a topological sort of the state DAG.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Names carry no dependency information; order must follow the state DAG.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Answer magnitudes are outputs, not the dependency structure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Random orders read garbage predecessors; retries cannot fix systematic inversion.

easy.prompt: What is a valid fill order for the 2D knapsack table?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Increasing i (outer) then w (inner), since row i reads row i−1.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Decreasing i from n to 1 with w increasing.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Increasing w outer, i inner, both from 0.

easy.hint: Next step: write the transition's two reads and check which rows they sit in.

So finishing row i−1 entirely before row i guarantees correctness; within a row, w order is free (2D version). Decreasing i reads uncomputed future rows. Diagonal order is unnecessary here since dependencies are purely row-backward, not diagonal-critical.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: w-outer/i-inner still works actually? No: it interleaves rows before predecessors finish — unsafe in naive full-table loops without care.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.body: L(i) = max over all j of L(j) ignoring values.

choices.label: D

easy.explanation: Extend the best valid predecessor (smaller value, earlier position), or start new at length 1.
easy.deepDive: Any increasing subsequence ending at i extends some predecessor j with smaller value (or starts fresh at length 1). Maximizing over valid predecessors gives the longest such extension — the optimal-substructure step. Blindly extending i−1 breaks when a[i−1] ≥ a[i]; ignoring values admits non-increasing picks; counting predecessors confuses count with longest length.

L(n) forces inclusion of the last element (wrong when it is small); L(1) forces the first; summing mixes incompatible anchored optima into a meaningless total.

easy.prompt: What is the 0/1-knapsack transition at state (i, w)?

easy.explanation: Each item is a binary decision; the cell takes the max of the skip-branch and the take-branch.
easy.deepDive: 0/1 choice is binary: skip keeps capacity w with items 1..i−1; take adds v_i and drops to capacity w−w_i with items 1..i−1. The optimum is the better of the two — the optimal-substructure step. Always-take, density-greedy, and single-best are all unsound for 0/1 (counterexamples: heavy valuable item blocking two medium ones).

easy.prompt: When is a greedy algorithm a candidate for provable optimality?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.body: The problem involves graphs.

easy.explanation: Greedy needs the greedy-choice property (plus optimal substructure): local-best first step is globally safe.
easy.deepDive: Greedy-choice means: take the locally best item (earliest finish, smallest coin, lightest edge) and some optimum still completes from there. Sorting, numeric output, and graphs are incidental — many greedy wins are unsorted/non-graph (Huffman), and many sorted/graph problems need DP. Without this property, greedy is just a heuristic.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sortedness aids efficiency but never justifies greedy safety.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Output shape is irrelevant to whether local choices compose optimally.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Greedy spans scheduling, coding, and matroids — far beyond graphs.

easy.prompt: What structurally separates greedy from dynamic programming?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Greedy builds one pass with irrevocable local picks; DP compares overlapping sub-decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Greedy is always slower than DP.

choices.label: C
choices.body: DP never gives optimal answers.

choices.label: D

easy.hint: Next step: count how many options each step keeps — one committed pick, or a max over branches?
easy.explanation: One committed local choice per step (greedy) versus maximizing over alternatives per state (DP).
easy.deepDive: Greedy commits per step (take earliest-finishing interval, merge rarest Huffman nodes) with no revisit. DP evaluates multiple options per state (take/skip) and keeps the max. Speed is not definitional — some greedies are slow, some DPs fast. Both target optimality; they differ in how many alternatives each step considers: one versus many.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Speed varies; the distinction is single-commitment versus maximizing over options.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DP is exactly the optimal-substructure workhorse; it routinely gives optima.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Their decision structures are opposites: commit-one versus compare-many.

easy.prompt: Unweighted activity selection: which interval should greedy pick next?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

easy.explanation: Earliest-finishing compatible interval minimizes blocked room — the optimal greedy rule.
easy.deepDive: Earliest-finish leaves maximum room for the rest — the exchange step swaps any optimum's first interval for this one without shrinking the schedule. Shortest-first fails (a short middle interval blocks two compatible longs); earliest-start locks in long blockers; fewest-overlaps is unproven and suboptimal on known instances. Sort by finish, then scan once: O(n log n).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A short interval can sit in the middle blocking two compatible longer ones.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Earliest start can select a marathon interval that blocks everything.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overlap-count sounds plausible but has counterexamples; finish-time is the proven rule.

easy.prompt: What is the optimal unweighted interval-scheduling algorithm?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sort by finish time; scan once, keeping intervals compatible with the last kept.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sort by start time; keep everything.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Check all subsets of intervals.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sort by length; keep the shortest half.

easy.hint: Next step: write the loop invariant — kept intervals are compatible and extendable to an optimum.
easy.explanation: Finish-sorted single scan with compatibility checks implements earliest-finish greedy in O(n log n).
easy.deepDive: Sorting (O(n log n)) puts earliest finishers first; one linear scan keeps an interval iff it starts at/after the last kept finish. Each keep is safe by the exchange argument, so the scan builds an optimum. Start-sorted keeping-everything admits overlaps; subsets are exponential; shortest-half is arbitrary. This sort-then-scan shape is the interval-scheduling template.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Start order with no compatibility check returns overlapping sets — invalid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Subset enumeration is exponential; greedy solves it in O(n log n).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Keeping a fixed fraction by length has no optimality basis.

easy.prompt: How does Huffman coding construct its tree?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Repeatedly merge the two least-frequent nodes; assign 0/1 to branches.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Split frequencies into two equal halves recursively.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Sort symbols alphabetically, then merge adjacent pairs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Merge the two most-frequent nodes first.

easy.hint: Next step: pull the two smallest weights off a min-heap, fuse them, and push the sum back.
easy.explanation: Bottom-up rarest-pair merging with a min-heap constructs the optimal prefix code.
easy.deepDive: Each merge creates a parent of summed weight with 0/1-labeled edges; repeating on a min-heap builds the optimal prefix tree bottom-up in O(n log n). Splitting is Shannon–Fano (suboptimal); alphabetical order ignores weights; merging most-frequent first buries common symbols deep — the exact inverse of optimal. The merge sequence also determines codeword lengths directly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Top-down halving is a different (suboptimal) Shannon–Fano scheme.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Alphabetical order carries no frequency information.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Merging most-frequent first maximizes weighted path length — backwards.

easy.prompt: Frequencies a:6, b:4, c:2, d:3. What Huffman code results?

choices.label: B
choices.body: All symbols get 2-bit codes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: a:0, b:1, c:00, d:01 (mixed prefix violations).

choices.label: D
choices.body: a:00, b:01, c:10, d:11 with a longest.

easy.hint: Next step: run three merges on the min-heap {2,3,4,6} and record each symbol's depth.
easy.explanation: Merges (c+d), (b+cd), (a+bcd) give depths 1,2,3,3 — frequent symbols get short codes.
easy.deepDive: Heap: merge c+d (2+3=5), then b+{cd} (4+5=9), then a+{bcd} (6+9=15). Depths: a=1, b=2, c=d=3 — frequent symbols shallow. Assigning 0/1 per branch gives a:0, b:10, c:110, d:111 (prefix-free). Fixed 2-bit codes waste a bit on a (frequency 6); option C is not prefix-free (a=0 prefixes c=00); option D inverts the frequency order.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Fixed-length ignores skew: a (frequency 6) deserves fewer than 2 bits on average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: a=0 is a prefix of c=00 — not a valid prefix code.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Giving the most-frequent symbol a longest code inverts optimality.

easy.prompt: What is the general shape of an exchange (greedy-stays-ahead) proof?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Start from any optimum; swap in the greedy choice without worsening it; repeat to reach greedy's output.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Show greedy is the fastest possible program.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Test greedy on every input by brute force.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Prove greedy choices are never locally optimal.

easy.hint: Next step: find the first place an optimum differs from greedy and try swapping in greedy's pick.
easy.explanation: Exchange proofs morph an arbitrary optimum into greedy's solution via harmless swaps, one choice at a time.
easy.deepDive: The exchange template: take an optimal solution differing earliest from greedy's, swap its first differing element for greedy's pick, and show feasibility + no-worse value. Iterating converts some optimum into greedy's exact output — proving greedy optimal. Speed benchmarks, exhaustive tests, and anti-local claims are not proofs; the swap-without-harm step is the entire content.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Running time is irrelevant to whether greedy's answer is optimal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Infinite input spaces cannot be brute-forced; proof must be general.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Greedy picks are locally optimal by construction; the issue is global safety.

easy.prompt: What is the exchange step for earliest-finish interval scheduling?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Replace the optimum's first interval with the earliest-finishing one: feasibility and count are preserved.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Delete the optimum's first interval without replacement.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Add the greedy interval on top of the full optimum.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sort the optimum by start time and stop.

easy.hint: Next step: compare greedy's first finish with the optimum's first finish — which leaves more room?
easy.explanation: Earliest-finish swaps into the optimum's first slot harmlessly, freeing at least as much room.
easy.deepDive: Let g be earliest-finishing and o the optimum's first-finishing interval; g finishes no later than o, so swapping g for o keeps all later intervals compatible (they start after o, hence after g). Count is unchanged (one-for-one) and feasibility holds — some optimum now starts with g. Repeating per step converts an optimum into greedy's schedule. Deletion shrinks count; addition creates overlaps; bare sorting proves nothing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Deletion drops the count by one — the swap must preserve cardinality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Adding without removing creates overlaps with the optimum's first interval.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sorting alone is not a proof; the swap-and-preserve step carries the content.

easy.prompt: What constitutes a counterexample to a greedy algorithm's optimality?

choices.label: A
choices.body: An instance where greedy returns a feasible but suboptimal answer.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An instance where greedy crashes with an error.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A proof that greedy runs in exponential time.

choices.label: D

easy.explanation: One input where greedy's feasible output is beaten by another feasible solution kills optimality.
easy.deepDive: Refuting greedy optimality needs one concrete input: greedy executes normally but its value is worse than a exhibited better feasible solution (e.g., coins {1,3,4} amount 6: greedy 3 coins vs. 2). Crashes disprove robustness, not optimality; slowness is complexity, not correctness; succeeding instances never refute a universal claim. Feasible-but-worse is the precise falsifier.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Crashing is a bug, distinct from returning a valid-but-suboptimal answer.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Running time does not address answer quality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Successes cannot falsify a for-all-inputs optimality claim.

choices.body: Layer 0: {s}; Layer 1: {a,b}; Layer 2: {c}

choices.label: B
choices.body: Layer 0: {s}; Layer 1: {a}; Layer 2: {b,c} if edge a-b exists and b-c exists

choices.label: C
choices.body: Layer 0: {s}; Layer 1: {a,b,c} all at once

choices.label: D

easy.hint: List s neighbors first as Layer 1, then unvisited neighbors of Layer 1 as Layer 2 — what is the distance of b if only reached via a?
easy.explanation: BFS assigns each node to the layer equal to its shortest-path distance (in edges) from s.
easy.deepDive: Trace queue: start [s]. Pop s, push a. Pop a, push b (b not reached via s directly). Pop b, push c. Layers record distance from s: dist[s]=0, dist[a]=1, dist[b]=2, dist[c]=3 in a line graph. BFS discovers in increasing distance because the queue is FIFO. Thus nodes one edge farther appear exactly one layer later.

wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Puts all nodes one hop away; only a is adjacent to s.

easy.prompt: In DFS, what is the difference between discovery time and finish time?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.body: Discovery = first visit (push); finish = all descendants done (pop)

choices.label: C
choices.body: Discovery = finish; they are two names for the same timestamp

choices.label: D
choices.body: Finish = time the node is first seen in the adjacency scan

easy.explanation: Discovery stamps entry to the recursive call; finish stamps exit after exploring the whole subtree.
easy.deepDive: Trace DFS on s-a line: clock 1 discover s, clock 2 discover a, clock 3 finish a, clock 4 finish s. So intervals nest: s=[1,4], a=[2,3]. Discovery and finish differ whenever a node has any work below it. Equality would hold only for isolated nodes with no recursion. The parenthesis structure is what enables cycle and topo reasoning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: No fixed +1 gap; the gap equals subtree size, e.g., s spans 1..4 above.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: They coincide only trivially; generally discovery < finish with descendants between.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: First-seen time is discovery, not finish.

easy.prompt: Which order is guaranteed topological for a DAG?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Any order of vertices

choices.label: B
choices.body: Increasing DFS discovery time

choices.label: C
choices.body: Decreasing DFS finish time

choices.label: D
choices.body: Increasing BFS layer then alphabetical

easy.hint: For edge u→v, which must finish first — and so which comes first in the output order?
easy.explanation: Every DAG edge goes from higher to lower finish time, so sorting finish descending is topological.
easy.deepDive: Trace DAG s→a, s→b, a→c, b→c. DFS from s: finish c=4? Actually discover s1,a2,c3,finish c4,finish a5,b6? then b7? Let's do systematic: s1,a2,c3,finish c4,finish a5,b6,finish b7? wait b→c black skip, finish b, finish s. Decreasing finish: s,a/b,c gives s first, valid. Increasing discovery also starts s but then a,c before b — still valid here yet fails generally. Only decreasing finish guarantees every edge u→v has finish[u]>finish[v].

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Arbitrary orders violate edges; e.g., c first breaks a→c.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Discovery order can place a descendant before an undiscovered ancestor sibling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: BFS layers ignore edge direction constraints across same-layer edges.

easy.prompt: What are Kosaraju's two passes?

choices.label: A
choices.body: DFS on G, then DFS on reversed G in decreasing finish order

choices.label: B
choices.body: BFS from each node and intersect reachable sets

choices.label: C

easy.explanation: Kosaraju's two passes isolate SCCs using finish-order on the transpose.
easy.deepDive: Trace: G: 1→2→3, 3→2, 4 alone. DFS finishes: 3? Actually 1→2→3 finishes 3,2,1 then 4. Decreasing: 1,2,3,4 (or 4 first). Reverse DFS from 1 reaches only {1}, from 4 reaches {4}, from 2 reaches {2,3} — the SCC. Increasing order would start at 3, leaking across SCCs in reverse graph. Topo sort fails on cyclic graphs. wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Increasing order processes sinks first and merges distinct SCCs.

easy.explanation: Every direct neighbor of s is discovered when s is dequeued, so each lands in Layer 1 with parent s.

easy.prompt: DFS recurses s into a into c. While c is being explored, what is on the recursion stack?

choices.label: A
choices.body: s, a, c from bottom to top of the stack

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only c; s and a already finished

choices.label: C
choices.body: s and c, with a already popped

choices.label: D

easy.explanation: Ancestors stay on the recursion stack until their whole subtree finishes, so the stack holds the full s-to-current path.
easy.deepDive: Trace: enter s (stack [s]), recurse to a ([s,a]), recurse to c ([s,a,c]). Nobody finishes until c's adjacency is scanned, so all three stay gray. Finishing unwinds c, then a, then s. Hence an active descendant implies every ancestor is still open. The stack exactly mirrors the current root-to-node path.

easy.prompt: Why must every finite DAG contain a node with indegree zero?

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

easy.hint: Start at any node and keep following an incoming edge backward — what would it mean if you never stopped?
easy.explanation: A backward walk cannot cycle in a DAG, so it must halt at a node with no incoming edges.
easy.deepDive: Start anywhere and follow any incoming edge backward. Finitely many nodes force either a stop at indegree zero or a repeated node. A repeat closes a directed cycle, contradicting acyclicity. Hence the walk must stop at a source. This source seeds Kahn's algorithm and inductive DAG proofs.

easy.prompt: What is the initialization plus the basic update step shared by Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford?

choices.label: B

easy.explanation: All shortest-path algorithms start from 0/∞ estimates and improve them by edge relaxation.
